name: Tzotzil, Huixtán
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.verdict: a reachable source states the stress pattern

earlier_scan.note: Root-initial stress, phrase-final prominence (general Tzotzil; glottocode retired into tzo)

new_statements.quote: El acento primario de una palabra tzotzil cae en la primera sílaba de la raíz; además hay un acento aun más fuerte que acompaña la última sílaba de una frase o una oración (puede consistir en una sola palabra, pronunciada aisladamente, o en palabras enunciadas con el mismo aliento). [...] Aquí el símbolo / representa el acento de la palabra, y el símbolo // representa el acento de la frase, que es todavía más enfático. Es claro que las partículas no se acentúan salvo que estén en la posición final.
new_statements.translation: The primary stress of a Tzotzil word falls on the first syllable of the root; in addition there is an even stronger accent that accompanies the last syllable of a phrase or a sentence (which may consist of a single word pronounced in isolation, or of words uttered in the same breath). [...] Here the symbol / represents word stress and the symbol // represents phrase accent, which is still more emphatic. Clearly, particles are not stressed unless they are in final position.
new_statements.citation: Haviland, John B. 1981. Sk'op sotz'leb: El tzotzil de San Lorenzo Zinacantán. México: Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Investigaciones Filológicas, Centro de Estudios Mayas. Capítulo I, 'Notas sobre la fonología'.
new_statements.locator: p. 14 (Cap. I, Notas sobre la fonología; PDF page 7 of the chapter scan; verified on the page image)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: Verified on the page image (PDF page 7 of = printed p. 14, running head "EL TZOTZIL DE SAN LORENZO ZINACANTAN"). Both quoted sentences are there exactly: "El acento primario de una palabra tzotzil cae en la primera sílaba de la raíz; además hay un acento aun más fuerte que acompaña la última sílaba de una frase o una oración (puede consistir en una sola palabra, pronunciada aisladamente, o en palabras enunciadas con el mismo aliento). Por ejemplo, véanse las frases siguientes:" followed by five examples with / and // marks (jvábajom//, li jvábajomé//, Chtál li jvábajomé//, Chtál xa li jvábajom ?uné//, ?Ali jvábajomé//, chtál xá//), then "Aquí el símbolo / representa el acento de la p…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the first syllable of the root (prefixes such as s-, ch-, j- are unstressed); a stronger phrase-level accent falls on the final syllable of the phrase or sentence, so a word in isolation is heard with final prominence. Delgaty & Ruiz Sánchez 1978 (San Andrés) p. 11 state the same root-initial rule and add that in long strings a further stress is inserted so that no more than three unstressed syllables occur in a row; Laughlin 1975 (Zinacantán) p. 23 says the same (isolated words: final; connected speech: root vowel, the first if two).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Haviland: none stated. Delgaty & Ruiz Sánchez 1978 p. 11: an additional stress is placed 'de manera que nunca aparezcan más de tres sílabas seguidas sin acento' (examples cha.c'ti.xu.bi.nun.cu.tic, li.vi.ni.que.ti.qué, marked orthographically for the reader).
new_statements.exceptions: Haviland: particles are unstressed unless phrase-final. Laughlin 1975 p. 23: in words in isolation primary stress is final 'except in affective verbs with -luh, first person plural exclusive suffixes, and reduplicated stems of two syllables', where it is marked with an acute accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Two-level system: word-level stress on the root-initial syllable vs. a stronger phrase/sentence-final accent (Haviland marks them / and //). Citation forms in isolation therefore show final prominence (Laughlin). Delgaty 1978 treats the sentence-final prominence as a pitch rise (with fall in main clauses, without fall in preposed subordinate clauses).
new_statements.identity_note: tzot1261 'Tzotzil, Huixtán' is a Glottolog bookkeeping entry for the retired ISO code tzu, merged into Tzotzil [tzo] = tzot1259 by ISO change request 2008-061. No Huixtán-specific phonology could be opened: the quoted statement is Haviland 1981 on the ZINACANTÁN dialect (Glottolog bookkeeping tzot1264), corroborated by Laughlin 1975 (Zinacantán) and by Delgaty & Ruiz Sánchez 1978 p. 11 (SAN ANDRÉS, tzot1260), whose introduction explicitly says Huixtán Tzotzil was left out of the dictionary 'por presentar diferencias considerables'. The only Huixtán description, Cowan 1969 (SIL PIL 18), was not accessible. by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) this statement belongs to the language entry tzot1259 and should not create a separate Huixtán entity; the Huixtán-specific rule remains unverified until Cowan 1969 is read.

sources.note: p. 11 'Sobre la Acentuación': 'Las palabras se acentúan sobre la primera sílaba de la raíz, sea ésta simple o compuesta. En cadenas de varias sílabas se acentúa otra sílaba más, de manera que nunca aparezcan más de tres sílabas seguidas sin acento'; sentence-final syllable gets a pitch rise-and-fall; stress therefore not. San Andrés dialect; Introducción p. xvii: 'El tzotzil de Huixtán no se ha incluido por presentar diferencias considerables.'

sources.citation: Laughlin, Robert M. 1975. The Great Tzotzil Dictionary of San Lorenzo Zinacantán. (Smithsonian Contributions to Anthropology 19.) Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press. xii+597 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: p. 23: 'Primary stress occurs on the final syllable of single words in isolation except in affective verbs with -luh, first person plural exclusive suffixes, and reduplicated stems of two syllables.. In normal speech, however, primary stress falls upon the root vowels (on the first, if there are two) and at the end of a phrase.' Zinacantán.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Tzotzil language', section 'Stress and intonation' (cites Laughlin 1975).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: 'In normal speech, stress falls on the first syllable of the root in each word, and the last word in a phrase is heavily stressed. For words in isolation, primary stress falls on the final syllable except in affective verbs with -luh, first person plural exclusive suffixes, and reduplicated stems of two syllables.' Second-hand paraphrase of Laughlin 1975 p. 23; no Huixtán information.
